en: Preface to the Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State The *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State* is the concluding scripture of the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Now, as for the discourse on *prajñā*, its duration is vast and its principles profound; there is nothing that does not sweep away emptiness to resolve obstructions, sever conceptualization to eliminate emotional attachments. This is truly because sentient beings...

Delusive attachments have long been deeply entrenched, making it difficult for true nature (*tathatā*) to manifest. Therefore, the Buddha did not discriminate between good and evil, defilement and purity, or their respective characteristics;
he refuted and rejected everything. Although true nature and its wondrous function are indeed present, he provisionally declared them non-existent.

Only when emotional attachments were forgotten and principles were relinquished, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization, did he then draw forth the inquiry of King Nigrodha and loftily proclaim the Dharma of the Five Patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*).

The net [of compassion] is the ultimate expression of the patriarch’s heart; it skillfully employs the chisel and hammer to secretly connect with the initial capacity of both the Separate and the Common Teachings, refining the profound path of both ordinary beings and sages.
Upon arriving at the *Lotus Sūtra*, which reveals and clarifies the truth, the family inheritance is entrusted to him, and the signless nature of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is pointed out.
All things thus constitute the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. When investigating the efficacy of this true mark, that efficacy arises from *prajñā*.
The essential point of *prajñā* is that it must be realized through wondrous awakening. Therefore, it is said: "The Infinite Meanings arise from a single Dharma. This is precisely what is meant.
Only our Tiantai Master Zhizhe deeply lamented that in future ages the kalpa would gradually decline, strife would become entrenched, and the conditions for *prajñā* would [diminish].

[The Master’s] Commentary. The Sūtra says: "If a nation is about to fall into chaos, the spirits and deities will first fall into chaos. Because the spirits and deities are in chaos, the myriad people will likewise fall into chaos.
When such calamities arise, one should receive, uphold, lecture upon, and recite this *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, the essential method for protecting the state lies especially in the exegesis of this sūtra; it was for this reason that the Great Master composed his commentary on the sūtra. Alas, as for this commentary...
It flourished extensively in海东 (Haidong) but was lost in China. In the past, the Venerable of Siming attempted to compose a commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* but did not succeed;
this was much like the Great Master of Tiantai, who prostrated himself before the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* yet failed to obtain it.

Was it not the case that the earnest resolve of those who sought the Dharma in earlier and later times shared the same principle? Fortunately, the Song dynasty monk Ruxun obtained it from a sea merchant, and Zhao Shuizhi provided a preface for it.
Although the *Jiǎnduān* is now recorded in the Dragon Canon (*Nanjing*), it has not been heard of at the lecture halls.
Recently, the Venerable Master Mǐn of Tiantái, in response to the invitation of various gentlemen in Wumen, resided at Beisì of Bào’ēn during the winter of the Wùxū year.

At that time, as the frontier regions were beset by many troubles and the subjects and citizens were unsettled, he was commissioned in the spring of the Jǐhài year to lecture on the *Rénwáng Hùguó Bōrě* [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra].

Regarding the sūtra, the version sought for the Buddha’s protection is that expounded by Master Weicheng and translated by Amoghavajra, which is currently the most widely circulated edition in the Tang dynasty.

As for the Great Master’s commentary, it is based on the version translated by Kumārajīva. While there are mutual differences and similarities between the two versions of the sūtra text, their essential purports are perfectly complementary.
Furthermore, in the Tripitaka editions, the sūtra and its commentary are each contained in separate volumes, making research difficult. Therefore, in accordance with...

Following the model of the great works of Tiantai and the precedent of the three combined editions of the *Avataṃsaka*, the sutra and its commentaries have been divided into fascicles and compiled into bound volumes.

The topical outlines (*ke*) are placed before the sutra, while the sub-commentary (*shu*) is appended after it. Punctuation has been added anew, so that the text may be analyzed with meticulous detail and made clear at a single glance upon opening the scroll.
Master Chenglian further consulted the Northern Edition of the Tripitaka for a complete collation, performing this task with palms joined in reverent devotion.
And he spoke in verse:
“Prajñā is like space; its merit is immeasurable. Entrusted to the various kings, may they receive it with faith according to the teaching.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.”
Upon hearing this sutra but once, they shall protect and uphold it for an instant;
They shall cause all calamities within their realms— Epidemics and the weapons of war—to be entirely eliminated.
Through the merit of giving the Dharma, they shall benefit all sentient beings, Causing them all to together resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Written on the day of the Universal Door Manifestation in the sixth month of the twenty-sixth year of the Guangxu era,
by the monk Chenglian, a junior disciple of the Tiantai school, at the western chamber of Ba’en North Temple in Wumen.
